clue.text: Things for sale — how I'm happy with that!

parts.note: goods are merchandise, things offered for sale

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper surveys the stock on offer and declares satisfaction with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'how' look like the start of the exclamation, but it is simply HOW, joined to GOODS.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of approval, the old-fashioned way of saying 'well done' or 'bravo'.

clue.text: I phone Leo about wine I enjoy

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone rings a friend called Leo to chat about a favourite wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges I PHONE LEO. The definition is spoken in the voice of the person meant: one who could say 'wine I enjoy' as a creed.
explanation.definitionFit: A connoisseur or lover of wine, from Greek roots for wine and fondness.

clue.text: Dog died — awkward situation

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for died, as in genealogies
to be in a hole is to be in a fix or awkward situation

explanation.surface: A pet's death leaves its owner in a difficult position.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild canine of Asia, also called the Asiatic red dog, which hunts in packs.

clue.text: Chemist, flamboyant type who may do business on the high street?

definitions.text: who may do business on the high street?

parts.note: Fritz Haber was the German chemist who devised the ammonia process
a dasher is a showy, stylish, dashing person

explanation.surface: A showy pharmacist might open up shop in the town centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chemist' suggests a pharmacy, but it is a named chemist, Fritz Haber. A haberdasher is a traditional shopkeeper; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in sewing goods such as ribbons and buttons, typically keeping a shop in town.

clue.text: Big dawn, silly prattler

indicators.note: silly suggests the words are muddled, so their letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: A garrulous person talks nonsense about a magnificent sunrise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' rearranges the letters of BIG DAWN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who talks at tedious length with little substance, an idle chatterer.

clue.text: Crook offering rubbish at auction?

definitions.meaning: a crook is a dishonest person, a rogue
a lot is an item put up at auction, so a worthless one is a poor lot

explanation.surface: A swindler sells off junk under the hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: A disreputable person, and literally a poor item in a sale room.

clue.text: British home's wine storage facility

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: An English house has its own wine cellar.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack or compartment in a cellar holding bottles, as in a numbered wine store.

clue.text: One providing strong drink to make girl calmer

parts.note: Di is a short girl's name (Diana)
stiller means quieter, calmer

explanation.surface: Someone gives a nervous young woman a stiff drink to settle her.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of spirits such as whisky or gin by distillation.

clue.text: Bit of tree healthier-looking when pollarded

indicators.note: pollarding cuts back the top of a tree, so the first letter of the word is lopped off

parts.note: rosier means healthier-looking, pinker in the cheeks

explanation.surface: Part of a tree looks in better shape after being cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when pollarded' removes the top letter, R, from ROSIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A willow shoot, cut for basket-making, is a pliant part of the tree.

clue.text: Unusually in Inverness, there's some fun coming

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words, so the answer lies within them

explanation.surface: A visitor to the Highlands is told an unusual amount of entertainment is on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' points to letters inside FUN COMING. The definition names a word used in Scotland, Inverness being a Highland city.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scots dialect adverb meaning remarkably or extremely, as in 'unco guid'.

clue.text: Forbid article proposin' a potential hazard

parts.note: to forbid is to ban
an is the indefinite article
the dropped g of proposin' signals the clipped form askin', as asking is proposing

explanation.surface: Someone casually suggesting marriage is warned of a pitfall.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in proposin' tells you to drop the G from ASKING too.
explanation.definitionFit: A slippery peel on which people proverbially slip, hence any pitfall waiting to trip someone up.

clue.text: Perform very quietly, drowned by a certain organ

indicators.note: something drowned by another is engulfed inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: the ear is an organ of hearing
pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quietly

explanation.surface: A musician plays so softly that a church organ drowns out the performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' suggests the instrument, but it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: To come on stage or take part in a show, as an actor does.

clue.text: Book of prayers? See cleric taking one into pub last thing on Sunday

indicators.note: into says one piece is placed inside the word for the pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub

indicators.note: the cleric taking one means the numeral is attached right after him

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a cleric
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the last thing on the word Sunday is its final letter

explanation.surface: A vicar, after the Sunday service, pops into the pub with a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last thing on' takes Y from SUNDAY. The question mark admits that a breviary holds offices and prayers rather than being just a prayer book.
explanation.definitionFit: The Catholic book of the daily divine office, containing psalms, hymns and readings for clergy.

clue.text: Remarkable cynic the age somehow engenders

indicators.note: somehow suggests these letters come together in some other way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sceptic of the times gives rise to something notable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges the eleven letters of CYNIC THE AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking enough to draw attention, as a bold design is.

clue.text: Proper perspective is something geometricians know about

parts.note: right means correct or proper
an angle on something is a point of view, a perspective

explanation.surface: Getting the correct viewpoint is something mathematicians understand.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninety-degree corner, a basic figure in the study of shapes.

clue.text: Like ancient library books, being narrow-minded

definitions.meaning: old volumes were often covered in leather, an animal skin binding
bigoted, rigidly stuck in old ways of thinking

explanation.surface: Old library volumes seem to share their keepers' conservative views.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally bound in leather, and figuratively stubbornly conventional and prejudiced.

clue.text: Track — dash one end to the other

indicators.note: the letter at one end of the word is shifted round to the opposite end

parts.note: elan is dash, flair or verve

explanation.surface: Someone sprints from one end of a running track to the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one end to the other' sends the opening E of ELAN to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow road or a marked strip for a runner or swimmer.

clue.text: Retailer in a dip in Gloucestershire town

indicators.note: in says one piece sits within the name of the town

parts.note: Newent is a small market town in Gloucestershire, an English county
a sag is a dip or droop

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper finds trade slumping in a small West Country town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a dip' reads like trade slumping, but 'in' is the container signal. Newent is a small Gloucestershire market town.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper selling papers and magazines is a kind of shop trader.

clue.text: Finish behind bishop's crook

indicators.note: the finish comes behind, placed after the abbreviation for bishop

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
an end is a finish

explanation.surface: A bishop's crozier is seen trailing at the close of a procession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bishop's crook' suggests the crozier, but 'crook' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To crook something is to curve it, as a finger is curved or a pipe is angled.

clue.text: Old coin that William and Mary each had?

definitions.text: Old coin that William and Mary each had?

parts.words: Old coin that William and Mary each had?
parts.note: William III and Mary II reigned jointly, so each held a share of the throne, punning on a pre-decimal British coin worth two shillings and sixpence

explanation.surface: A numismatic query about the joint monarchs of seventeenth-century England.
explanation.walkthrough: The coin was a British piece worth two shillings and sixpence, withdrawn in 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-decimal coin, and literally the share of the throne owned by each joint monarch.

clue.text: Spots officer coming up with drinks

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Col is short for Colonel, an officer
ales are drinks of beer

explanation.surface: A senior officer arrives with a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns COL to LOC.
explanation.definitionFit: Places or settings, the sites where events happen.

clue.text: Repeatedly exclude one cold and brutal

indicators.note: repeatedly means the word for exclude appears twice over

parts.note: to bar is to exclude
I is the Roman numeral for one
C stands for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Someone keeps being shut out, alone in the cold, which feels cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Savagely cruel and uncivilised, like a savage horde.

clue.text: Little creatures drowning in potomac (a river)

indicators.note: the creatures are immersed within the words that follow, lying inside them

explanation.surface: Tiny animals perish in an American river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drowning in' hides the word across POTOMAC A RIVER. The grid as held prints ACAPI, but the hidden letters spell the real word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mites and ticks, tiny arachnids, collectively in zoological Latin.

clue.text: First half of dance — a foot gets stuck in this dress

indicators.note: a piece that gets stuck in another is lodged inside it
the first half of the word for a dance is just its opening three letters

parts.note: the cancan is a high-kicking dance

explanation.surface: A dancer's foot gets caught in her long robe mid-routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The dance is the cancan, so its first half is a word in its own right. 'this dress' reads as the definition; only 'dress' is, with 'this' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A long loose tunic of the Middle East, or a woman's flowing robe in that style.

clue.text: Football club managed to bring in money once

indicators.note: one piece brings in the other, holding it inside

parts.note: to run a team is to manage it

explanation.surface: A football club managed to attract investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' tells you this currency is no longer used; France replaced it with the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: The former currency of France and Belgium, replaced by the euro.

clue.text: What justified a war for Caesar?

definitions.text: What justified a war for Caesar?

parts.words: What justified a war for Caesar?
parts.note: the Latin phrase, as a Roman such as Caesar would put it, for the event that provokes or justifies going to war

explanation.surface: A historical question about Julius Caesar's grounds for his campaigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for Caesar' signals the Latin phrase, still used in English for a pretext for war.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for an occasion of war, the act that gives grounds for hostilities.

clue.text: What's picked up by the leader in front?

definitions.text: What's picked up by the leader
definitions.meaning: the leader of an orchestra, the principal violinist, picks up a stick strung with horsehair to play
the forward end of a ship

explanation.surface: A question about what the person at the head of things takes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' here is the orchestra's leader, the first violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: A violinist's horsehair-strung stick, and the forepart of a vessel.

clue.text: Cuts lines at fourteen's

definitions.meaning: chops or slashes, as in budget reductions
the x and y reference lines of a graph meet each other at the figure in 14-across, perpendicularly

explanation.surface: Lines are cut where they meet a given number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fourteen' refers to the answer at 14-across: graph axes meet at ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Chops or eliminates, and the reference lines of a coordinate graph.

clue.text: Bereaved woman will entertain any number if there's an opportunity

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a widow is a woman whose husband has died
N stands for an unspecified number in mathematics

explanation.surface: A widow will entertain any number of suitors given the chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entertain' suggests hospitality, but it puts N inside WIDOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A window is a brief period when a chance is open, as in a launch window.

clue.text: Insight shown by Muslim ruler in southern metropolis?

indicators.note: in places the ruler inside the combined southern city

parts.note: a city is a metropolis
an aga is a Muslim commander or ruler in the Ottoman empire

explanation.surface: A Muslim ruler in a southern city shows great understanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisdom and keen judgment, the quality of a sage.
